segments.title: Why carriers were a difficult treaty category
segments.summary: Carrier limits were difficult to design because the ships were still experimental and their military value was unsettled in 1921-22.
segments.body: Aircraft carriers posed a particularly awkward problem for the Washington Treaty. Early carriers were few, experimental, and often incomplete, so negotiators had little reliable evidence for deciding what counted as a carrier or how much capability a tonnage allowance bought. The Royal Navy could classify nearly every carrier before Courageous as experimental, making replacement rules and treaty accounting unusually flexible. Conversion allowances created another difficulty because an inherited hull could consume more treaty tonnage for less aviation capacity than a purpose-built ship.

evidence.note: The transcript describes early carriers as experimental and explains the conversion problem.

segments.title: Carrier ratios and Japan’s strategic position
segments.summary: The treaty’s carrier allocation could make Japan feel relatively weaker as carrier aviation became more important.
segments.body: The original 5:5:3 carrier ratio becomes more contentious when France and Italy are included. A numerical compromise that seemed tolerable while carriers were unproven could grow politically sharper as naval aviation gained importance. Japan's carrier allocation was smaller than the combined French and Italian allowance even though neither European navy was its principal anticipated opponent. The perceived imbalance helps explain the Japanese shift of reconnaissance capacity to cruiser-borne aircraft, preserving scarce carrier tonnage for duties that only carriers could perform.

evidence.note: The ratio comparison links carrier allocations to Japanese reconnaissance and planning choices.

segments.title: The Washington Treaty’s carrier tonnage rules
segments.summary: A close reading of the carrier articles shows how total allowances, the 27,000-ton cap, and conversion exceptions constrained fleet design.
segments.body: The treaty set national carrier allocations, a normal individual limit of 27,000 tons, and an exception for two ships of up to 33,000 tons. Two large conversions could consume so much of a national allowance that little room remained for other carriers, especially under Japan's 81,000-ton total. The quoted articles also limited heavy guns while leaving smaller anti-aircraft weapons unrestricted, reflecting uncertainty about whether carriers might still fight more like gun-armed capital ships. Worked examples turn the legal totals into plausible fleets, showing that even Britain and the United States would have little room after building two large ships and two ships at the normal maximum.

evidence.note: The transcript quotes Articles 7, 9, and 10 and works through the fleet consequences of their tonnage limits.

segments.title: The development path from Cuckoo to Swordfish
segments.summary: Reliable carrier torpedo attack emerged through years of aircraft, weapon, and release-system refinement rather than arriving fully formed.
segments.body: Second World War torpedo-bombing performance cannot be projected back into the early 1920s. Aircraft range, release accuracy, and torpedo reliability were all still developing when the Washington Treaty was negotiated. The path from the Sopwith Cuckoo to the Fairey Swordfish included wooden stabilizing fins and later tension-cable arrangements for the torpedo. These refinements explain why treaty delegates could not yet treat a carrier air group as a reliably ship-killing force.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the iterative technical changes that made later aerial torpedo drops reliable.

segments.title: How treaty wording permitted large new-build carriers
segments.summary: Article 9 encouraged conversion of existing capital ships but did not legally require the two permitted 33,000-ton carriers to be conversions.
segments.body: Article 9 uses permissive wording where a binding conversion rule might be expected. The treaty said powers "may" use two ships otherwise due for scrapping to obtain the larger carrier allowance. That language encouraged economical conversion but did not require it. Britain, the United States, and Japan could therefore have built two purpose-designed 33,000-ton carriers from scratch in the 1920s, establishing a different technical baseline for naval aviation.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes the treaty's permissive legal language from the expectation that powers would convert existing hulls.

segments.title: Why purpose-built carriers used tonnage better
segments.summary: Comparing Furious, Eagle, Hermes, and Hōshō shows why purpose-built carriers could carry more aircraft for the same treaty tonnage.
segments.body: Furious, Eagle, Hermes, and Hōshō are compared through tons per aircraft rather than displacement alone. Converted hulls carry the inherited compromises of their original design, while purpose-built ships can devote more of their footprint to hangars and aircraft handling. Hermes and Hōshō therefore appear markedly more tonnage-efficient than the larger conversions available to treaty planners. Under a total-tonnage treaty, that efficiency translates directly into more operational aircraft for the same legal allowance.

evidence.note: The comparison gives displacement and aircraft-capacity calculations for early converted and purpose-built carriers.

segments.title: Why the Royal Navy avoided routine deck parking
segments.summary: North Atlantic and North Sea weather made exposed aircraft an unreliable basis for Royal Navy carrier-capacity planning.
segments.body: British and American carrier-capacity figures are difficult to compare when one navy routinely counts deck parks and the other does not. Royal Navy experience had shown that aircraft left exposed could be lost to heavy weather in the North Atlantic and North Sea. Although deck parking was practical in the Mediterranean, British planners wanted an air group that could survive deployment wherever the carrier was sent. Hangar footprint therefore mattered more to British capacity estimates than a maximum fair-weather deck load.

evidence.note: The transcript links Royal Navy deck-parking policy to aircraft losses in northern waters.

segments.title: Why larger carriers gain hangar efficiency
segments.summary: As a carrier grows, fixed systems consume a smaller proportion of its hangar footprint and leave more room for aircraft.
segments.body: Usable hangar footprint matters more than displacement alone. Islands, funnel trunks, lifts, offices, and access routes occupy space on every carrier regardless of air-group size. On a larger hull, those fixed demands consume a smaller proportion of the available length and beam. The resulting efficiency helps a large purpose-built carrier support more aircraft and maintenance space than a proportionally scaled conversion.

evidence.note: The transcript explains how hangar footprint, islands, funnels, and lifts affect capacity as carrier size changes.

segments.title: How early arresting wires kept aircraft on the deck
segments.summary: Furious's sloped deck and longitudinal wires show how early landing aids first tried to prevent aircraft from sliding over the side.
segments.body: HMS Furious shows how early flight decks and landing aids differed from mature carrier practice. Her rounded bow and rising after deck were intended to smooth airflow and help landing aircraft lose speed by climbing a slope. Early arresting cables ran longitudinally, chiefly to keep an aircraft from skidding over the deck edge. Later transverse wires performed the more familiar job of bringing the aircraft to a halt, completing the shift toward mature carrier landing systems.

evidence.note: The transcript describes Furious's deck profile and contrasts early longitudinal cables with later transverse arresting wires.

segments.title: British deck-edge lift studies - and their limits
segments.summary: Personal papers suggest that designers considered external lifts for large British carrier conversions, but no approved plan establishes that the idea would have been built.
segments.body: British designers normally preferred internal lifts, but personal papers and constructor discussions include external or deck-edge lifts for a possible Admiral-class or G3 strike-carrier conversion. Moving a lift to the deck edge could preserve valuable internal hangar footprint on a roughly 30,000-ton ship. No surviving approved plan confirms that the idea progressed beyond discussion. The surviving evidence supports an exploratory interpretation and does not show that the Royal Navy committed to build it.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses possible external lifts for Admiral-class or G3 conversions and stresses the absence of a confirmed plan.

segments.title: Why 27,000 tons changed the carrier trade-off
segments.summary: Scaling a purpose-built carrier toward 27,000 tons could combine a larger air group with armour, while a 22,000-ton design bought Britain a sixth hull under the historical allowance.
segments.body: A projection from Hermes and Hōshō suggests that a 27,000-ton purpose-built carrier could conservatively support about 52 aircraft. Ark Royal and Implacable show how rapidly capacity and protection improve with scale: Ark Royal carried roughly 72 aircraft on about 22,000 standard tons, while a larger design could approach 70-80 aircraft and add armour. Ark Royal's strong flight and hangar decks are presented as a step toward the armoured Illustrious and Implacable designs. The countervailing treaty incentive was numbers, since building at about 22,000 tons let Britain fit six carriers into 135,000 tons. Procurement therefore became a fleet-level choice between individual survivability and air-group power on one side and another available deck on the other.

evidence.note: The transcript compares projected air-group capacity, armour, and the sixth-carrier benefit of building at about 22,000 tons.

segments.title: Carrier aviation before the strike-carrier era
segments.summary: Early carrier value lay in scouting, counter-reconnaissance, spotting, and trade protection as much as in striking enemy ships.
segments.body: The Royal Navy wanted carrier numbers for trade protection, reconnaissance, and fleet protection before reliable ship-killing aviation was available. British assessments of Jutland and other operations gave German aerial reconnaissance an important role, strengthening the case for fighters that could suppress enemy scouting. Carrier aircraft could also find enemy forces and spot the fall of shot for battleships beyond direct visual range. The Blackburn Blackburn functions here as a sensor node in a distributed weapon system: the aircraft supplied information while the battleship delivered the destructive effect. The importance attached to these missions helped the Royal Navy maintain the world's largest operational carrier force until wartime losses changed the balance.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses carrier numbers, trade protection, counter-reconnaissance, and gunnery spotting.

segments.title: How imperfect carrier data shaped treaty choices
segments.summary: Conversion estimates looked poor because treaty planners had only early-carrier evidence, even though Lexington and Saratoga later performed better.
segments.body: A conversion based on Furious and Eagle is estimated to need about 38,500 tons to carry 52 aircraft. Lexington and Saratoga later beat that estimate, so the figure is not a universal law of conversion design. Its value is historical: these were the kinds of numbers available while the treaty was being negotiated. Technically minded navies could reason carefully and still make rules from an immature evidence base.

evidence.note: The transcript gives the 38,500-ton conversion estimate, contrasts Lexington and Saratoga, and frames the calculation as treaty-era information.

segments.title: HMS Eagle as a carrier-flagship model
segments.summary: Eagle's island anticipated flag-officer accommodation and offered a model for commanding a squadron from a larger British carrier conversion.
segments.body: HMS Eagle's island was designed with the possibility of carrying a flag officer and staff, even though the accommodation was limited and seldom used. That makes the ship more than an early conversion example: she provides a visible reference for how a larger British carrier could combine flight control with squadron command. Eagle also supplies the model for an imagined Admiral-class or G3 conversion equipped as a carrier flagship. The island's size reflected command functions as well as funnels, navigation, and flight-deck operations.

evidence.note: The transcript explains Eagle's limited flag accommodation and uses her island as a model for a larger British conversion.

segments.title: Why HMS Eagle might have remained HMS Cochrane
segments.summary: Retaining the Cochrane name would have linked an early British carrier to Thomas Cochrane's reputation for naval innovation.
segments.body: HMS Eagle began as the Chilean battleship Almirante Cochrane before conversion for the Royal Navy. Retaining Cochrane as the carrier's name would have tied the new ship to Thomas Cochrane's reputation for innovation. Early British naval aviation could then have used him as a historical figure around whom to build its identity. Eagle was also an apt name and later became strongly associated with aircraft carriers, so the choice illustrates how ship names can shape institutional memory within a counterfactual.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Eagle's Almirante Cochrane origin and discusses Thomas Cochrane as an innovative namesake for British naval aviation.

segments.title: A proposed equitable carrier treaty
segments.summary: The alternate treaty carries a 10:10:7:4:4 capital-ship ratio into carrier limits while avoiding fractional ship allowances.
segments.body: The proposed settlement carries the video's earlier 10:10:7:4:4 capital-ship ratio into carrier allocations. Fractional ship allowances are rejected because they add complexity and make equality depend on multiplying abstract ratios into much larger fleets. A 33,000-ton individual maximum comes directly from the historical treaty's exception, although applying it generally produces far larger totals than the actual agreement. The result is explicitly counterfactual and tests whether transparent whole-ship ratios could better satisfy the strategic requirements of all five powers.

evidence.note: The transcript derives the alternative whole-ship ratio and explains the 33,000-ton individual limit.

segments.title: How carrier islands supported faster flight operations
segments.summary: British carrier islands combined command, aircrew organization, and smoke management while protecting scarce hangar space.
segments.body: HMS Hermes shows why early British carriers devoted substantial volume to their island structures. Briefing and organizing pilots near the flight deck helped aircrew reach aircraft quickly when a launch was ordered. A tall island also carried funnel outlets high enough to reduce smoke interference over the deck. Experience with Argus, Eagle, Furious, Courageous, and Glorious taught the Royal Navy that funnel trunks passing through the hangar imposed a serious penalty on aircraft space.

evidence.note: The transcript connects island volume, pilot readiness, smoke clearance, and hangar-space efficiency.

segments.title: Continuous construction as industrial deterrence
segments.summary: A treaty that sustains shipbuilding capacity could leave every signatory more modern while reducing hopes of an easy challenge.
segments.body: The counterfactual broadens from carrier totals to the industrial effects of arms-control rules. Continued Allied construction would preserve shipyards, design experience, and successive generations of modern ships rather than allowing capacity to atrophy. Continued Japanese construction would also leave room for planners to hope that qualitative improvements could offset numerical inferiority, giving them a reason to remain within the system. Germany and Italy would then confront a Royal Navy whose fleet and construction base looked much harder to overtake, changing the deterrent calculation before war began.

evidence.note: The transcript links continuing treaty construction to industrial capacity, fleet renewal, and deterrence.

segments.title: Conversion deadlines and carrier service lives
segments.summary: Staged conversion requirements would preserve existing investment while delaying unrestricted purpose-built carrier construction.
segments.body: The alternate rules require carriers completed through 1926 to be conversions and require at least two conversions in each navy's programme through 1930. This protects capital already committed to hulls and long-lead machinery while preventing an immediate race for wholly new 33,000-ton ships. Pre-treaty experimental carriers could retire from 1930, later conversions from 1934, and new builds would remain for at least eighteen years. The timetable uses replacement policy to spread technical change across several generations instead of trying to freeze carrier development.

evidence.note: The transcript specifies conversion deadlines, retirement dates, and an eighteen-year life for new carriers.

segments.title: Hōshō and Japan's early carrier advantage
segments.summary: Hōshō gave the Imperial Japanese Navy an unusually efficient early platform for reconnaissance and fleet support.
segments.body: Hōshō appears as one of the most efficient early light-carrier designs despite the limitations expected of a first effort. At launch, her air group could provide reconnaissance and fleet support that the United States Navy would have had to take seriously. Her purpose-built layout gave Japan an early practical advantage over navies still relying heavily on conversions. The advantage was temporary as larger ships overtook her, but it demonstrates that early carrier competence did not develop evenly across navies.

evidence.note: The transcript assesses Hōshō's early reconnaissance value and design efficiency.

segments.title: The alternative carrier tonnage allocations
segments.summary: The proposed totals give Britain and the United States 330,000 tons each, Japan 231,000, and France and Italy 132,000 apiece.
segments.body: The 10:10:7:4:4 ratio produces national carrier-tonnage ceilings of 330,000 tons each for Britain and the United States, 231,000 for Japan, and 132,000 each for France and Italy. Every navy may build individual carriers up to 33,000 tons, subject to the earlier conversion and service-life rules. The 132,000-ton figure follows the earlier calculation and four ships at the individual maximum. The later spoken recap is rendered as 142,000 tons, which conflicts with that arithmetic. These totals create choices about fleet count and ship size rather than prescribing a uniform carrier design.

evidence.note: The earlier calculation explicitly raises the French and Italian allocations to 132,000 tons each.
The recap gives the British, US, and Japanese totals plus the 33,000-ton maximum, but renders the French and Italian figure as 142,000 tons.

segments.title: Why Italy could concentrate carriers and France could not
segments.summary: The same treaty allowance could support concentrated Italian air power in the Mediterranean but left France choosing between large ships and enough decks for three regions.
segments.body: The same 132,000-ton allowance creates different force structures because geography matters. Four 33,000-ton carriers could give Italy a concentrated aviation advantage inside the Mediterranean, where the Regia Marina expected to operate them together. France also had Mediterranean commitments but needed carrier availability in the Atlantic and Far East, making four large decks a poor fit. Six roughly 22,000-ton French carriers offer a way to distribute presence across those theatres. The comparison shows that nominal treaty equality did not produce equal operational choices.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Italian concentration in the Mediterranean with French requirements in the Mediterranean, Atlantic, and Far East.

segments.title: The Royal Navy's three-fleet carrier arithmetic
segments.summary: Twelve 27,500-ton carriers offered Britain a compromise between three-fleet distribution, air-group efficiency, and individual fighting power.
segments.body: Britain's 330,000-ton allowance could buy ten 33,000-ton carriers, eleven 30,000-ton ships, twelve 27,500-ton ships, or about fifteen at 22,000 tons. The Royal Navy's three-fleet structure made twelve or fifteen attractive because the force could be divided evenly among operating areas. The larger ship used its hangar and maintenance space more efficiently and was more likely to survive against a 33,000-ton opponent. Twelve 27,500-ton carriers, four per fleet, are presented as the best compromise between deck numbers, aircraft capacity, and protection. The tons-per-aircraft method is a reconstructed table checked against calculations being made in the 1920s, so it reflects a contemporary planning approach rather than an official fleet programme. Treaty tonnage functioned as a force-structure budget as well as a cap on individual designs.

evidence.note: The transcript works through four British fleet-size options and links the preferred twelve-carrier force to three operating areas.

segments.title: Lexington conversions and Japan's large-carrier option
segments.summary: Conversion rules probably preserve Lexington and Saratoga, while Japan's larger allowance opens a path to seven individually powerful carriers.
segments.body: Conversion rules make it likely that the United States still completes Lexington and Saratoga as carriers. Japan's 231,000-ton allowance, meanwhile, could support seven nominal 33,000-ton ships, with actual displacement perhaps creeping toward roughly 35,000 tons. Contemporary Japanese yards had ample experience with ships heavier than this, although balancing a carrier remained a distinct architectural challenge. The result is a counterfactual Japanese force of fewer but individually powerful decks, not a prediction that one exact design was inevitable.

evidence.note: The transcript retains Lexington conversions and considers Japanese carriers nominally limited to 33,000 tons but possibly heavier in practice.

segments.title: US carrier choices for two oceans
segments.summary: Atlantic and Pacific commitments let the United States choose between ten very large carriers, more medium carriers, or a mixed conversion and new-build programme.
segments.body: The United States faced a different distribution problem because its principal division was between Atlantic and Pacific fleets. Ten 33,000-ton carriers could be split five per ocean, while eleven 30,000-ton ships or twelve 27,500-ton ships would trade individual scale for more flexible allocation. A mixed programme is another option: large Lexington conversions followed by 27,500-ton new builds between 1926 and 1930. The choice remains open because it depends on what US planners believed carriers would do as well as the available tonnage.

evidence.note: The transcript compares US two-ocean allocations and considers a mixed programme of large conversions and medium new builds.

segments.title: How carrier missions changed from 1920 to 1926
segments.summary: Reconnaissance, air defence, and spotting dominated the 1920 mission set; strike became a larger design consideration only as the decade progressed.
segments.body: Carrier doctrine cannot be read backward from 1945 into 1920. In the immediate postwar period, reconnaissance, fleet air defence, and gunfire spotting were the core jobs, with only limited anti-submarine attacks against boats caught on the surface. Strike begins to enter the mission set around 1926 as aircraft and weapons mature. This changing purpose matters because a navy choosing carrier size and numbers was also choosing which evolving missions it could sustain across the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the 1920 reconnaissance, air-defence, spotting, and limited anti-submarine mission set with strike's emergence by 1926.

segments.title: A British 27,500-ton carrier programme
segments.summary: A 27,500-ton British new build offers a compromise between carrier numbers, useful air groups, and the protection of later armoured designs.
segments.body: The proposed British programme keeps smaller Courageous-class conversions while using a 27,500-ton new design as a practical middle course. This size could support a decent air group and useful protection without committing the fleet entirely to very large ships. An early design would probably place its strength and armour deck below the hangar, preserving the hull if the upper carrier structure suffered bomb damage. Repeated construction at that displacement would give the Royal Navy several design generations before the Second World War, trading maximum individual size for a sustainable three-fleet force.

evidence.note: The transcript develops the 27,500-ton new build, its protection concept, and a sustained replacement programme.

segments.title: How carrier growth could reshape Fleet Air Arm control
segments.summary: A much larger carrier fleet would make Air Ministry control harder to reconcile with the Royal Navy's operational needs.
segments.body: Sustained construction of numerous carriers would alter the institutional struggle over British naval aviation. The Royal Air Force as a service is distinguished from the Air Ministry, whose assumptions often constrained the Fleet Air Arm. One Air Ministry concept treated carriers as transports that could deliver land-based aircraft to the Far East and then send naval aircraft ashore to reinforce expeditionary air operations. That single-service logic risked leaving the fleet without the aircraft needed for reconnaissance, air defence, and strike work, making control of naval aviation an operational question as well as a bureaucratic one.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes RAF and Air Ministry positions and describes a carrier transport concept that would strip aircraft from the fleet.

segments.title: G3 conversions as a strike-carrier force
segments.summary: Converting four lightly started G3 hulls would trade total carrier numbers for a core of powerful strike carriers.
segments.body: The second British programme cancels the smaller Furious path and treats four lightly started G3 battlecruisers as treaty conversions. Long-lead items had already been ordered, so the ships could enter service relatively quickly despite little hull structure having been completed. Four roughly 30,000-ton conversions would reduce the total number of carriers but give the Royal Navy a persistent core of strike carriers alongside later 27,500-ton fleet carriers. The replacement timetable reaches a 1942 peak that would require careful retirement timing to remain within the tonnage ceiling.

evidence.note: The transcript compares the G3 conversion programme's carrier count, strike strength, and replacement timing.

segments.title: What a G3 carrier conversion might enable
segments.summary: A G3 conversion could combine a large flight deck, substantial hangar space, flagship facilities, and the possibility of operating larger aircraft.
segments.body: Eagle and Ark Royal provide reference points for adapting a G3 hull without relocating its machinery. Its 260-metre length and broad hull could support a very large flight deck, multiple lifts, maintenance space, and a carrier-squadron flagship role. Funnel positions would shape an island farther aft than on historical Royal Navy carriers, making the proposal a design departure as well as a conversion. A deck roughly 260 to 270 metres long might also make twin-engine naval aircraft practical as engines improved, permitting greater payload and performance while leaving contemporary reliability debates unresolved.

evidence.note: The transcript examines G3 dimensions, conversion layout, and possible twin-engine operations.

segments.title: Treaty limits, security, and deterrence
segments.summary: The closing argument is that an arms-control system endures only when it provides security and an incentive for every power to keep it.
segments.body: The conclusion connects carrier rules to the larger political purpose of treaty design. Peace cannot rest on freezing construction so tightly that states feel exposed while technology changes around them. The treaty era is compared with the years after HMS Dreadnought, when powers could absorb new technology through normal construction and better judge their relative positions. A durable settlement needs enough preparedness to make aggression too costly while avoiding an imbalance that encourages pre-emption through fear or opportunism through perceived weakness. Treaty compliance lasts when each state believes its security and future advantage are better served by keeping the agreement than by abandoning it.

evidence.note: The transcript links treaty compliance, security, continued construction, and deterrence.
